title: Bibliometric analysis and systematic review of sisal fiber treatment and reinforcement in mortar and concrete
abstract: Abstract The global construction industry faces increasing pressure to reduce its environmental footprint and adopt sustainable alternatives to conventional materials. Natural fiber-reinforced composites have emerged as promising solutions, with sisal fiber in particular attracting significant attention for its abundance, renewability, biodegradability, and favorable mechanical properties. Extracted from the leaves of Agave sisalana, sisal fiber offers a cost-effective and eco-friendly reinforcement option for mortar and concrete. Research findings indicate that incorporating sisal fibers into cementitious composites can substantially improve performance by enhancing tensile and flexural strength, impact resistance, crack-bridging ability, and overall toughness, while also reducing brittleness and contributing to weight reduction. From a sustainability perspective, sisal fiber reinforcement reduces reliance on non-renewable synthetic fibers and supports the development of environmentally responsible construction practices. Despite these advantages, several challenges hinder its widespread application. Fiber degradation in the alkaline cement matrix, insufficient fiber matrix bonding, and variability in fiber properties often compromise long-term performance. To overcome these limitations, different treatments and modifications such as alkali treatment, silane application, and hybridization with other fibers have been proposed to enhance interfacial adhesion, durability, and mechanical efficiency. This review systematically synthesizes current knowledge on sisal fiber-reinforced mortar and concrete, with particular emphasis on mechanical performance, durability, and sustainability. It critically examines the challenges and limitations associated with sisal fiber application while highlighting recent advances in fiber treatment techniques. Furthermore, the review identifies research gaps and future opportunities for optimizing sisal fiber utilization in construction materials. By consolidating existing findings, this study provides a comprehensive reference for researchers, engineers, and practitioners seeking to design sustainable, high-performance cementitious composites that align with global efforts toward greener construction practices.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The use of agricultural byproduct for cement and concrete [ 1 ,  2 ]– [ 3 ] and the escalating global demand for sustainable, lightweight, and high-performance materials has catalyzed a paradigm shift away from traditional synthetic reinforcements toward renewable natural fibers [ 4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Among the diverse array of plant-based fibers, sisal (Agave sisalana) has emerged as one of the most promising for composite applications, owing to its exceptional combination of mechanical properties, widespread availability, low cost, and minimal environmental impact. Sisal fiber exhibits tensile strengths ranging from 400 to 700 MPa, Young’s moduli of 9–22 GPa, and a low density of approximately 1.45 g/cm³, which translates into specific mechanical properties that compare favorably with those of E-glass fiber [ 8 ,  9 ]. With an annual global production exceeding 4.5 million tonnes, sisal is cultivated extensively in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly Tanzania, Brazil, China, and Kenya, providing economic opportunities for developing nations while simultaneously supplying a renewable feedstock for the composites industry [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ].

The hierarchical structure of sisal fibers comprising crystalline cellulose microfibrils oriented at a characteristic angle of 20–25° relative to the fiber axis, and embedded within an amorphous matrix of hemicellulose and lignin is responsible for their unique mechanical behaviour. Cellulose content typically ranges from 55% to 78%, while hemicellulose and lignin constitute 8–19% and 2–11%, respectively [ 12 , 13 ]. This architecture imparts not only strength and stiffness but also a degree of toughness and energy absorption capacity that distinguishes sisal from many other natural fibers. Consequently, sisal fiber-reinforced composites have been extensively investigated across a broad spectrum of matrix systems, including thermoplastics (polypropylene, polyethylene, polylactic acid), thermosets (epoxy, polyester, vinyl ester), cementitious matrices, and elastomers [ 8 , 12 ]. Applications now span automotive components such as door panels, boot liners, and underfloor paneling construction materials, including roofing sheets, cement reinforcement, and insulation boards; aerospace interior paneling, marine structures; and consumer goods ranging from furniture to electronic device casings [ 14 , 15 ].

Despite these promising attributes, the widespread adoption of sisal fibers in high-performance engineering applications remains constrained by three interconnected challenges: inherent hydrophilicity, which leads to poor interfacial adhesion with hydrophobic matrices; severe degradation in alkaline environments characteristic of cementitious systems; and high moisture absorption, which causes dimensional instability and compromises long-term durability [ 13 ,  14 – 15 ]. The hydrophilic nature of sisal fiber arises from abundant hydroxyl groups on cellulose chains, rendering the fiber surface polar and wettable by water but incompatible with non-polar polymer matrices. This incompatibility results in weak fiber–matrix bonding, inefficient stress transfer, and premature composite failure, with interfacial shear strength values for untreated sisal–epoxy systems typically ranging from 0.18 to 0.30 MPa [ 10 ]. Furthermore, the alkaline pore solution of Portland cement (pH 12.5–13.5) initiates progressive degradation through multiple mechanisms: alkaline hydrolysis of lignin and hemicellulose, depolymerization of cellulose chains via peeling-off reactions, and mineralization through precipitation of calcium hydroxide within fiber lumens and cell walls [ 16 , 17 ]. Accelerated ageing studies have demonstrated that untreated sisal fibers embedded in Portland cement lose up to 86% of their tensile strength after only 30 wet–dry cycles, with complete loss of reinforcing capacity occurring within two years of service. Additionally, sisal fibers can absorb up to 200% of their own weight in water, leading to swelling, micro-cracking at interfaces, plasticization of amorphous components, and accelerated biological and chemical degradation [ 18 , 19 ].

Recognizing these challenges, researchers have devoted substantial effort to developing mitigation strategies that can be broadly categorized into fiber surface treatments, matrix modifications, and hybrid reinforcement architectures [ 16 ,  17 ]– [ 18 ]. Fiber surface treatments constitute the most extensively investigated approach and include alkali treatment with sodium hydroxide to remove amorphous components and increase surface roughness silane coupling agents that create chemical bridges between fiber hydroxyl groups and matrix functional groups; acetylation to replace hydrophilic hydroxyl groups with hydrophobic acetyl moieties; polymer coating using styrene butadiene, epoxy, or polyester to provide protective barriers; plasma treatment to modify surface chemistry without affecting bulk properties; and nanoparticle grafting with materials such as cellulose nanocrystals, iron oxide, or manganese dioxide to introduce hierarchical roughness and enhanced mechanical interlocking [ 19 ,  20 ,  21 – 22 ]. Each of these methods has demonstrated varying degrees of success in improving interfacial adhesion, reducing water absorption, and retarding alkaline degradation, with reported improvements in interfacial shear strength ranging from 35% to 120% and tensile strength retention after ageing increasing by up to 384% [ 16 , 23 , 24 ].

Matrix modification, particularly for cementitious systems, has proven equally effective. Partial replacement of Portland cement with pozzolanic supplementary cementitious materials such as metakaolin, fly ash, silica fume, or rice husk ash reduces the calcium hydroxide content and lowers the alkalinity of the pore solution, thereby mitigating fiber degradation. Yimer and Gebre [ 24 ] demonstrated that replacing 30 wt% of cement with metakaolin extended the service life of sisal fibers in cementitious composites by a factor of 13.7, while rice husk ash at the same replacement level increased fiber tensile strength retention after 30 wet–dry cycles by 384%. These improvements are attributed to the consumption of calcium hydroxide through pozzolanic reactions, the formation of additional calcium silicate hydrate gel that densifies the interfacial transition zone, and the reduced concentration of hydroxyl ions that slows the kinetics of cellulose depolymerization [ 9 ]. Hybrid composites, combining sisal with glass fibers or with other natural fibers such as hemp, jute, or banana, offer a balanced compromise between mechanical performance, cost, and sustainability [ 25 ]. Reported that hybrid sisal glass composites with a stacking sequence of three sisal layers and two glass layers achieved tensile strengths 84% higher than pure sisal composites while maintaining 70% of the flexural modulus of all-glass composites at 40% lower density. Multi-scale reinforcement strategies integrating microcrystalline cellulose or nanocellulose with macro-scale sisal fibers have further demonstrated synergistic improvements in both strength and fracture energy, with reporting an 18.4% increase in compressive strength and a 100% increase in fracture energy for cementitious composites containing 0.1 wt% microcrystalline cellulose and 0.5 wt% sisal fibers [ 26 ].

Despite these substantial advances, the existing literature suffers from several critical gaps that limit the rational design and industrial translation of sisal fiber composites. First, previous reviews have largely focused on either polymer matrix composites or cementitious systems in isolation, without integrating findings across these distinct material families or developing unified design principles to guide treatment selection based on application- specific requirements. Second, reported treatment parameters vary widely across studies, with NaOH concentrations from 0.5% to 30%, treatment times from 10 min to 72 h, and temperatures from ambient to 150 °C, without standardized protocols or a mechanistic understanding of optimal processing windows. Consequently, contradictory recommendations abound, and there is no comprehensive framework to predict treatment outcomes based on fiber provenance, matrix chemistry, or desired performance characteristics. Third, long-term durability under realistic service conditions involving coupled environmental stressors, such as moisture cycling, temperature variation, ultraviolet radiation, freeze-thaw action, and chemical attack, remains severely understudied, with most investigations limited to accelerated laboratory ageing over short timeframes. Degradation kinetics models, such as those developed by [ 30 ] for cellulose in alkaline media, have not been extended to predict service life under field conditions or to account for synergistic effects of multiple degradation mechanisms. Fourth, emerging areas, including life cycle assessment of sisal production systems, integration of sisal waste-to-energy technologies, and development of fully bio-based hybrid composites, have not been adequately incorporated into mainstream composites research, resulting in a disconnect between laboratory-scale property optimization and holistic sustainability evaluation. Finally, the translation of laboratory successes to industrial applications faces persistent barriers, including fiber quality variability, scalability of treatment methods, processing compatibility, and cost- effectiveness, yet systematic analyses of these translational challenges are lacking.

Unlike the other review papers [ 9 , 16 , 27 ,  28 ,  29 ]– [ 30 ] this article addresses these gaps by providing a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary analysis of sisal fiber reinforced composites that integrates findings across matrix systems, treatment methodologies, and performance metrics. Specifically, this review offers several unique contributions an integrated comparative framework that systematically evaluates treatment efficacy across polymer, cementitious, and hybrid matrices using standardized performance indicators. a mechanistic synthesis of alkaline degradation pathways and their dependence on fiber microstructure, matrix chemistry, and environmental conditions. critical assessment of emerging technologies including plasma polymerization, cellulose nanocrystal electrophoretic deposition, and nanoparticle grafting, with comparative analysis of their cost-effectiveness, scalability, and environmental impact. analysis of multi-scale and hybrid reinforcement strategies, identifying synergistic mechanisms and optimal composition windows. integration of durability data, field exposure studies, and life cycle assessment to provide a holistic sustainability evaluation. Practical design guidelines distilled from the reviewed literature to support treatment selection, processing optimization, and quality control and identification of priority research directions to guide future investigations. By bridging fundamental materials science with engineering applications and sustainability considerations, this review aims to accelerate the development of high-performance, durable, and truly sustainable sisal fiber composites for next-generation structural and semi-structural applications.

sections.heading: Search String Used in Search Refinement (PRISMA Diagram)
paragraphs: The following keywords string was applied:  “ sisal fiber treatment and use in cement, concrete and mortar ”.  This ensured the retrieval of publications explicitly focusing on sisal fiber treatment and its application in cement, mortar, and concrete.

sections.heading: Access period
paragraphs: The search covered works published within the last 25 years, i.e. 2000 to 2025, capturing both early studies and recent advancements.

sections.heading: Subject area
paragraphs: The results were limited to subject areas relevant to cement-based composites and fiber treatments, primarily Materials Science (614), Engineering (180), Chemistry (69), and Chemical Engineering (17). However, few research outputs were included from Environmental Science, Agricultural and Biological Sciences, and Physics.

sections.heading: Document type
paragraphs: Retrieved publications were distributed across Articles (619), Conference Papers (143), Book Chaps. (54), Reviews (40), and Others (24).

sections.heading: Research output selection
paragraphs: Of the initial 888 publications, 31 were manually excluded: duplicates, irrelevant works (e.g., publications focusing only on textiles, unrelated polymers, or outside cement-based systems), and publications not written in English. From the remaining 857 publications relevant to sisal fiber treatment, a total of 61 articles (34 from Scopus and 24 from other sources) were selected based on citation and relevance of the paper.

sections.heading: The Total Link Strength of co-authorship links for countries
paragraphs: The Total Link Strength (TLS) is an essential measure of international research collaboration, quantifying the intensity of co-authorship links between countries. A higher TLS indicates stronger collaborative networks, reflecting the extent to which researchers in a country are engaged in joint publications [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ]. Figure  5  shows that India, Brazil, and the United Kingdom are the top three contributors to research on sisal fiber and its use. India leads with the most publications and collaborations, focusing on enhancing fiber durability and performance in sustainable composites and construction materials. Brazil, as a major sisal producer, contributes substantially through studies of mechanical properties, durability, and large-scale applications in eco-friendly buildings. The United Kingdom complements these efforts with advanced testing, modelling, and sustainability assessments, thereby strengthening international collaboration. Collectively, these countries play a central role in advancing knowledge and promoting sisal fiber as a sustainable material.

sections.heading: The Co-occurrence analysis of keywords in publications
paragraphs: Co-occurrence analysis of keywords is a vital bibliometric method for uncovering the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of a research field [ 31 , 32 ]. Figure  6  shows keywords co-occurrence in sisal fiber research. Among the clusters,  “ natural fibers” is the dominant term, with the largest node, reflecting its central role in the field. Notably, “sisal” occurs close to “natural fibers,” highlighting its strong association with the broader research theme. This close linkage suggests that sisal fiber is increasingly recognized as a key material within the natural fiber family, particularly in studies of composite materials, chemical modification, durability, and sustainability. The prominence of sisal alongside natural fibers indicates growing research interest, as scholars explore its potential for sustainable construction, reinforcement, and eco-friendly composites. This trend demonstrates that sisal fiber is gaining visibility and importance in academic discourse, aligning with global efforts to develop sustainable materials.

paragraphs: The VOS viewer map in Fig.  7  shows that five journals dominate research on natural fibers and composites. The Journal of Applied Polymer Science and the Journal of Materials Science are central to polymer modification and fiber matrix studies, while the Journal of Reinforced Plastics focuses on reinforcement and mechanical performance. Construction and Building Materials leads in applied civil engineering research, and Materials Today Proceedings captures a large share of conference-based work. Together, they represent the core outlets linking the use of natural fiber to practical building applications.
Fig. 7 Total link strength according to sources

The bibliometric analysis reveals a rapidly evolving research landscape for sisal fiber composites, characterized by three interconnected dimensions: thematic concentration around “natural fibers” as the dominant keyword hub with “sisal” positioned in close proximity, confirming its emergence as a key material within sustainability and chemical modification research clusters; publication outlet distribution identifying five core journals Journal of Applied Polymer Science, Journal of Materials Science, Journal of Reinforced Plastics, Construction and Building Materials (the leading applied civil engineering outlet), and Materials Today Proceedings that collectively bridge fundamental materials science with practical construction applications; and international collaboration analysis through Total Link Strength mapping identifying India (leading in publication volume and collaborative intensity), Brazil (leveraging its geographic advantage as a major sisal producer), and the United Kingdom (contributing advanced testing and sustainability assessments) as the dominant collaborative triangle that synergistically addresses the entire value chain from fiber production to end-use application, while the notable absence of other major sisal-producing countries (Tanzania, China, Kenya) from the top collaboration network reveals a critical gap in geographic representation. Collectively, these bibliometric dimensions demonstrate that sisal fiber research has matured from scattered individual studies to a coherent, internationally collaborative field with clear thematic direction, established publication channels, and growing emphasis on sustainability and practical implementation, while simultaneously revealing gaps in geographic representation and knowledge integration that future research must address through enhanced South-South collaborations and standardized testing protocols.

sections.heading: The use of sisal fiber for cement mortar and concrete
paragraphs: The incorporation of sisal fibers into cement mortar and concrete has been shown to significantly enhance their mechanical performance. Following the integrative framework proposed in this review, this systematic synthesis reorganizes the existing literature on sisal fiber-reinforced cement mortar and concrete according to five analytical dimensions, namely, an integrated comparative evaluation of treatment efficacy, mechanistic understanding of degradation pathways, a critical assessment of emerging modification technologies, multi-scale and hybrid reinforcement strategies, and holistic sustainability integration. The analysis draws on laboratory-based mechanical testing, microstructural characterization, durability assessments, and comparative studies across geographic contexts, including Asia, Africa, and South America.

The literature permits direct comparison of treatment methodologies using standardized performance indicators such as compressive strength gain, flexural or tensile strength improvement, workability change, and durability outcome [ 35 ]. Alkaline treatment yields a 12.83% increase in compressive strength and a 14.92% increase in tensile strength, but raises environmental disposal concerns [ 9 ]. Pozzolana treatment offers comparable mechanical gains, superior durability, and lower environmental impact. Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) treatment improves both tensile and compressive strength while enhancing corrosion resistance [ 34 , 35 ]. Dual polymer coatings reduce porosity and improve the fiber-matrix bond [ 36 , 37 ] while a biomimetic approach combining sisal fibers with  Bacillus subtilis  produces notable improvements in compressive (+ 14%), tensile (+ 36.8%), and flexural (+ 30.9%) strengths, coupled with reduced shrinkage and permeability [ 38 ]. Across all treatments, the efficacy ranking from highest to lowest is: biomimetic > pozzolana > alkaline > dual coatings > untreated. However, direct cross-study comparisons are compromised by varying fiber content, curing regimes, and testing standards a methodological gap that requires harmonization protocols.

The primary degradation pathway for sisal fibers in cementitious matrices is the alkaline hydrolysis of lignin and hemicellulose, driven by the high pH (12–13) of the cement pore solution. The literature shows a critical dependence on three factors: fiber microstructure, matrix chemistry, and environmental conditions. Sisal’s hierarchical cell wall structure determines alkali penetration pathways; untreated fibers exhibit rapid alkalization through lumen and pit channels, leading to mineralization and embrittlement within 28–90 days [ 39 ]. Pozzolanic additives such as fly ash or rice husk ash reduce pore solution pH by consuming calcium hydroxide, thereby mitigating degradation [ 40 , 68 ]. No long-term field exposure studies (> 1 year) are reported in the reviewed corpus, representing a critical knowledge gap regarding environmental conditions. The hydrophilic nature of sisal fibers induces localized shrinkage cracks at the fiber-cement paste interface, yet paradoxically the same water absorption creates a bridging effect that restrains crack propagation in the bulk matrix [ 39 ]. The net mechanical outcome depends on fiber content and dispersion quality, with optimal ranges identified at 0.5–2.0% by cement mass [ 41 ].

A critical assessment of emerging technologies reveals wide variation in technology readiness level (TRL), scalability, cost-effectiveness, and environmental impact. Alkaline treatment (NaOH) is highly scalable and inexpensive but raises disposal concerns (TRL 7–8) [ 9 ]. Pozzolana treatment offers moderate to high efficacy with low environmental impact but has medium scalability (TRL 6–7). Dual polymer coatings achieve high porosity reduction but are batch processes with high material costs (TRL 3–4) [ 36 , 37 ]. Biomimetic bacteria-based treatment gives very high mechanical gains but requires culture maintenance and has very low scalability (TRL 2–3) [ 38 ]. Hornification improves tensile strength and pull-out resistance using only water cycling, offering very low environmental impact and medium scalability (TRL 4–5) [ 42 ]. Nanocrystalline cellulose combined with dispersing agents enhances hydration and reduces porosity, but remains at the laboratory-scale with high production cost (TRL 2–3) [ 43 ]. Importantly, plasma polymerization and nanoparticle grafting are not reported in the reviewed corpus for cementitious systems. Overall, the most scalable treatments provide only moderate performance or raise environmental concerns, while high-performance emerging technologies face significant barriers to industrial adoption. No reviewed study provides techno-economic analysis or scaling projections—a priority research gap.

Reinforcement operates at three hierarchical length scales. At the micro-scale, individual sisal fibers (diameter 100–300 μm, length 10–50 mm) provide crack bridging at 10–100 μm crack widths, with pull-out behaviour governed by frictional bond strength [ 42 ]. At the meso-scale, woven sisal fabrics exhibits strain-hardening behaviour and multiple cracking under tensile and flexural loads, approaching the performance of synthetic textiles [ 44 , 45 ]. At the macro-scale, limited evidence exists for structural applications, though pervious concrete [ 60 ] and recycled aggregate systems [ 46 ] demonstrate feasibility. Hybridization strategies further enhance performance: combining sisal with polypropylene fibers improves toughness and mechanical strength after ageing through microstructural densification [ 41 ] sisal with microcrystalline cellulose and dispersing agents enhances hydration and reduces porosity while improving carbonation resistance [ 59 ] sisal with fly ash (0.5% fiber content) gives long-term strength improvements [ 40 ] and sisal with rice husk ash increases strength, cracking resistance, and impermeability [ 47 ]. From the synthesized data, the optimal sisal fiber content in cementitious composites is 0.5–2.0% by cement mass. The precise optimum depends on workability tolerance (fiber content > 1.5% typically requires superplasticizers for self-compacting concrete [ 48 ]) strength priority (compressive strength peaks at lower content 0.5–1.0%, while flexural strength and toughness continue improving up to 2.0% [ 49 ]), and durability requirements (combined treatments allow higher fiber content without degradation). No study systematically maps the three-dimensional response surface of fiber content, fiber length, and treatment type.

Durability data from the reviewed literature derive almost exclusively from accelerated laboratory tests. Water absorption is reduced across all treated fiber composites [ 50 ,  51 ]– [ 52 ] acid resistance improves with alkaline-treated fibers though disposal concerns are noted [ 9 ] carbonation resistance is enhanced with microcrystalline cellulose and dispersing agents [ 43 ] corrosion resistance improves with Na₂CO₃ treatment [ 34 , 35 ], and long-term durability after ageing is maintained in hybrid sisal-polypropylene systems [ 41 ]. Critically, no reviewed study reports field exposure data exceeding twelve months for sisal fiber-reinforced cementitious composites. Freeze-thaw resistance and chloride ingress are not systematically evaluated. This absence of field validation represents the single most significant barrier to engineering adoption. Regarding life cycle assessment, only one comparative study is reported: sisal fibers demonstrate superior environmental performance relative to synthetic fibers (polypropylene, glass), though with moderate mechanical strength gains and a 20% workability reduction [ 18 ]. No study reports cradle-to-gate embodied carbon for treated versus untreated sisal, comparative LCA of different treatment methods, end-of-life scenarios (biodegradation, recyclability, downcycling), or the water footprint of fiber processing.

Drawing practical design guidelines from the synthesized literature, treatment selection should follow a pathway for standard construction without special durability requirements, the use of untreated sisal fiber at 1.0% by cement mass for enhanced durability under environmental constraints, employ pozzolanic treatment combined with fly ash at 0.5% fibers for maximum strength in laboratory or specialty applications, adopt biomimetic treatment with  Bacillus subtilis  and for corrosion-prone environments, Na₂CO₃ treatment is recommended. Processing optimization suggests fiber lengths of 25–50 mm for mortar and 40–60 mm for concrete, pre-wetting to counteract workability loss [ 39 ], and superplasticizer addition for fiber content exceeding 1.5% in self-compacting mixes [ 48 ]. Quality control is hampered by the absence of standardized fiber quality metrics (moisture content, aspect ratio distribution, surface functionality) and non-destructive evaluation methods for fiber dispersion in the hardened matrix.

A systematic synthesis of visual, durability, recycling, and treatment evidence, Fig.  9  confirms that sisal fiber inclusion effectively arrests crack formation and propagation within concrete matrices, an effect attributed to the bridging action of fibers that transfers stress across microcracks and enhances overall composite toughness [ 53 ,  54 ,  55 ]– [ 56 ]. Durability assessments reveal that a 1.5% fiber content improves resistance to acid attack and wetting-drying cycles while reducing permeability and shrinkage [ 57 ]. Additional studies report consistent gains in tensile strength and toughness, though compressive strength improvements are inconsistent and workability depends on fiber length and dosage [ 16 ]. Early-age compressive strength may increase, but this is accompanied by higher absorption and reduced flowability [ 58 ]. Other work notes tensile and flexural gains at the expense of slump and air content [ 59 ], with strength development slowing over time despite early improvements [ 24 ]. From a sustainability perspective, sisal fiber composites incorporating recycled aggregates provide sufficient flexural strength for semi-structural applications [ 64 , 65 ] exhibit superior mechanical performance and multi-cracking behavior, and are cost-effective compared to synthetic fibers [ 62 ]. Waste valorization is further supported by evidence that treated sisal residues improve bonding, flexural strength, and overall mechanical performance, with wet-dry cycles enhancing compatibility [ 10 , 67 , 68 ] while foundational studies confirm significant improvements in toughness, flexural strength, durability, low energy consumption, and ecological benefits, rendering sisal fibers suitable for structural applications [ 47 , 69 , 70 ]. Critically, treatment methods strongly influence performance: high fiber contents (up to 8%) improve flexural strength and fracture toughness with good fiber-matrix bonding observed via SEM, although high water absorption remains problematic [ 67 ] conversely, untreated fibers increase water absorption and permeability, reducing durability and underscoring the necessity of treatment [ 68 , 69 ]. To address these limitations, urea and EDTA treatments significantly improve flexural strength, densify the interface, and enhance cement hydration, yielding high-performance composites [ 70 ], and fiber morphology plays a measurable role, with irregular cross-sections improving adhesion strength up to 0.92 MPa, thereby enhancing bond and cracking resistance [ 65 ]. Overall, this body of evidence confirms that sisal fiber reinforcement, when properly treated and optimized for content and morphology, delivers robust crack control, durability under aggressive exposure, and sustainability benefits, though trade-offs with workability and long-term strength development require continued optimization.

As shown in Fig.  10 , the main limitation of natural fibers is their degradation when exposed to cement and concrete. Therefore, some studies recommend using sisal fibre, which offers environmental and economic benefits, to protect it from degradation. Overall, these studies show that untreated sisal fibers compromise durability and workability, but chemical and physical treatments, up to the optimum percentage as shown in Figs.  11  and  12 , along with morphological optimization, can greatly improve fiber-matrix bonding, durability, and overall mechanical performance.

sections.heading: Treatment of sisal fiber
paragraphs: Several studies have explored treatment methods to enhance the performance and durability of sisal fibers in cement-based composites. Physical treatments, such as wet-dry cycling or Hornification, have been shown to increase tensile and bond strength, as well as ductility, while reducing water absorption and dimensional instability, making them an environmentally friendly approach [ 10 , 67 , 68 ]. Thermal treatments, including thermal and high-temperature conditioning, have improved the tensile and flexural strength of sisal FRP composites, enhanced confinement capacity, and promoted durability, while offering sustainable alternatives to synthetic fibers [ 76 , 77 ]. Chemical methods remain widely applied, with alkali treatments the most common. These often enhance compressive, tensile, and flexural strength, though effectiveness varies with concentration and fiber brittleness [ 78 , 79 ]. Alternative chemical modifications, such as esterification, silane coupling agents, sol-gel processes, and organosolv pulping, have improved bonding, stability, and resistance to degradation [ 71 ]. Other innovative approaches, such as Sulphur infiltration, impregnation with timber-derived compounds, or incorporation in MgO-SiO 2  matrices, have also been found to enhance durability, bonding, and fracture resistance [ 80 ]. Some mixed treatments, such as paraffin oil immersion, have demonstrated improved thermal resistance but reduced mechanical strength due to increased porosity [ 81 ,  82 ,  83 ,  84 ,  85 ]– [ 86 , 87 ]. Overall, while chemical treatments significantly improve fibre-matrix interaction, their environmental and economic drawbacks highlight the potential of physical and thermal methods as more sustainable solutions [ 88 ].

As shown in Fig.  12 , there is a notable difference in the optical images of untreated and treated sisal fibers. Except for the alkali-treated samples, no significant changes were observed in the fibers’ surface morphology. After alkali treatment, however, the fiber surface roughness increased considerably, and the fibers appeared to have smaller diameters, likely due to the removal of hemicellulose and lignin [ 46 , 89 , 89 ]. Furthermore, as shown in Fig.  12 , this process eliminates natural binding materials and waxy substances that usually cover the fiber surface, thereby exposing more cellulose microfibrils. Nevertheless, increased surface roughness improves mechanical interlocking and enhances fiber-matrix adhesion when used in cementitious composites. Additionally, the reduction in diameter increases the fibers’ aspect ratio, further improving stress transfer and crack-bridging capacity in reinforced concrete [ 4 ]. Similarly, S. Thepruttana [ 40 ] shows, in Fig.  12 , SEM images of treated and untreated sisal fibers and demonstrates the effectiveness of alkali treatment and a natural rubber latex coating in modifying the surface morphology of sisal fibers. Alkali treatment reduces impurities on the fiber surface and enhances fiber stability, while the natural rubber latex coating provides a protective layer and facilitates the adherence of expanded perlite [ 7 , 10 , 48 , 79 , 90 ]– [ 92 ]. These modifications hold significant promise for enhancing the compatibility of Fibres with cementitious matrices, ultimately leading to improved mechanical performance in fiber-cement composites [ 7 , 10 , 48 , 79 , 90 ,  91 ,  92 ,  93 – 94 ].
Fig. 12 Optical microscopy images of sisal fiber after different treatments ( a ) untreated ( b ) silane ( c ) NaOH, and (d) NaOH +silane [ 7 ]

As shown in Fig.  11 , alkali treatment is recommended as a crucial pretreatment for sisal fibers intended for use in cementitious composites. By effectively removing surface impurities and partially eliminating hemicellulose and lignin, alkali treatment enhances fiber strength, stability, and dimensional consistency. For further improvements in fiber-matrix adhesion and composite performance, subsequent surface modifications, such as a natural rubber latex coating and the incorporation of particulate fillers, such as expanded perlite, are advised. Implementing these treatments can significantly improve the mechanical performance and durability of sisal fiber-reinforced cement-based materials. Sisal fiber treatments play a key role in improving fiber properties and compatibility with cementitious materials. Surface modifications enhance fiber stability, bonding, and protection, leading to better integration within composites [ 24 , 42 , 72 , 72 ,  73 ,  74 ,  75 ,  76 ]– [ 77 ].

Similarly, XRD analysis in Fig.  13  reveals that treated sisal fibers exhibited lower water absorption than untreated fibers. Both aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (AM)- treated and untreated mortars contain higher amounts of anhydrous phases, confirming that fibers absorb part of the water required for cement hydration, an effect more pronounced in untreated fibers. However, improper treatment can damage the fiber surface, as observed with AM treatment, which increased water absorption instead of reducing it. Mineralogical changes were also noted as the portlandite content decreased in Mortar with Sisal Fiber (M-SF-1) and Mortar with Sisal Fiber treated with AM (M-SF-AM-1). In contrast, calcite content increased in mortars treated with Urea (M-SF-UR-1) and Ethylenediaminetetraacetic Acid (M-SF-EDTA-1), a result of portlandite carbonation into calcite, accompanied by water release. Overall, sisal fiber demonstrates strong potential as a sustainable reinforcement for cement and mortar, provided that surface treatments are carefully controlled to enhance fiber matrix interaction, durability, and composite performance [ 70 ,  10 , 26 , 78 ,  79 ,  80 ,  81 ,  82 – 83 ].

sections.heading: Chemical treatments
paragraphs: The primary purpose of chemical treatment of natural fibers is to modify and optimize their surface characteristics, thereby improving their compatibility with cementitious or polymeric matrices. Among the different approaches, alkali treatment is the most widely applied because it effectively removes surface impurities such as waxes, oils, and lignin, while cleaning the fiber surface and exposing the underlying cellulose. This surface modification not only increases surface roughness but also enhances the availability of reactive hydroxyl groups, both of which contribute to stronger fiber matrix adhesion, and these are clearly illustrated by Figs.  14  and  15 . The modification of fiber surfaces through treatments such as alkali, silane, or other chemical processes plays a critical role in achieving durable, efficient, and high-performing natural fiber composites [ 24 , 84 , 85 , 86 , 87 ]. Chemical treatment remains the most widely studied, including alkali treatment with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) [ 88 , 24 ] sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) [ 24 ] paraffin oil [ 84 ] and sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) [ 84 ]. Advanced chemical modifications, such as silane coupling agents [ 89 ] and combinations with urea, EDTA, and ammonium salts [ 90 ] have also been explored to improve durability and fiber-matrix bonding.
Fig. 14 SEM Result of Alkali hot treatment ( a ) 0% ( b ) 2% ( c ) 4% (d) 6% ( e ) 8%, and ( f ) 10% NaOH [ 93 ]

A hybrid approach used in different studies, such as combining alkali treatment with pozzolana was reported by [ 91 ] while [ 89 ] integrated alkali treatment with wastewater recycling to mitigate chemical waste. Beyond purely chemical methods, thermal and hybrid treatments have also been studied [ 92 ]. Chemical, thermal, and hybrid approaches have been reported to yield variable improvements in strength and durability, depending on the treatment combinations. Physical treatments, such as boiling and washing, have been applied in combination with pozzolana admixtures, thereby offering a low-cost and eco-friendly alternative [ 91 ].

Chemical modifications remain prevalent, including alkali soaking [ 4 , 99 ], silane treatment [ 4 ], polymeric coatings such as Carboxylated styrene-butadiene rubber (XSBR) [ 78 , 79 ], natural rubber latex with perlite [ 40 ], and microwave-assisted alkali treatment [ 112 ], all of which enhance adhesion, reduce water absorption, and optimize composite strength. Physical treatments, particularly wetting-drying cycles, improve tensile strength, fiber-matrix adhesion, and dimensional stability in an environmentally friendly manner [ 113 , 114 , 22 ]. Thermal treatments, such as autoclave exposure, can reduce water absorption but may decrease tensile and bond strength if not carefully controlled [ 58 ]. Hybrid approaches, combining chemical treatment with fiber orientation or hybridization strategies, have been shown to further improve flexural and tensile strength while reducing water absorption [ 113 , 114 ]. Review studies also emphasize that these treatment methods, ranging from alkaline and surface modifications to interaction with superplasticizers and fiber orientation control, consistently enhance fiber-matrix bonding, mechanical performance, and durability while supporting the sustainable and eco-friendly use of sisal fibers [ 115 , 108 , 73 ]. Among the reviewed studies, most employed chemical treatments such as alkali (NaOH, Na₂CO₃), silane, esterification, and polymeric coatings, highlighting chemical modification as the most commonly used method to enhance fiber-matrix bonding, mechanical strength, and durability [ 7 , 57 , 116 ,  117 ,  118 ,  119 – 120 ].
Fig. 15 SEM Result of Alkali hot treatment ( a ) 0% ( b ) 2% ( c ) 4% ( d ) 6 % ( e ) 8%, and (f) 10% NaOH [ 93 ].

Figure  14  shows that untreated jute fabric, with a high concentration of hydroxyl groups and surface impurities such as pectin and wax, exhibits poor adhesion to epoxy resin and limited development of tensile strength. In contrast, hot-alkali treatment significantly improves fiber-matrix interfacial compatibility. Treated fibers show almost no pull-out or gaps within the epoxy, and fiber dispersion in the resin is markedly enhanced. On the other hand, some studies explored hybrid treatments that combined chemical and physical methods, where synergistic improvements in both mechanical and durability properties were observed [ 94 ,  95 ,  96 ,  97 ,  98 ,  99 ,  100 – 101 ].

Untreated sisal fibers contain natural impurities such as hemicellulose, lignin, and waxes, which increase water absorption, reduce fiber matrix bonding, and limit the durability and mechanical performance of cementitious composites. As shown in Fig.  14 A and B, the SEM image of the untreated sisal fiber reveals surface impurities, including hemicellulose, lignin, and waxes, which appear as deposits on the fiber surface. These impurities increase water absorption and reduce adhesion to the cementitious matrix, limiting the composite’s performance [ 102 ,  103 ,  104 – 105 ]. In contrast, the SEM image of the fiber treated with 20% NaOH (indicated by red circles) reveals significant surface damage, including fiber erosion and structural degradation, resulting from excessive chemical dosage (Table  1 ).

Therefore, both untreated and over treated fibers present disadvantages, emphasizing the importance of determining an optimum treatment level [ 102 ].

Generally, chemical treatments can improve fiber performance by removing impurities, enhancing surface roughness, and strengthening adhesion to the cement matrix, thereby reducing water absorption and improving overall stability. However, excessive chemical treatment may damage the fiber structure, reduce mechanical integrity, and negatively affect composite behaviour. Therefore, determining an optimum treatment is essential to balance impurity removal with the preservation of fiber strength, ensuring enhanced fiber matrix interaction, durability, and overall performance in sisal fiber reinforced cement and mortar [ 13 , 102 , 110 ,  111 – 112 ].

sections.heading: The effect of treated sisal fiber on the performance of concrete
Workability
paragraphs: Treated sisal fibers improve mechanical performance (e.g., flexural strength, crack bridging, pull-out resistance) by increasing surface roughness, removing weak surface layers (hemicellulose, lignin) via alkali treatments (NaOH, Na₂CO₃), or applying polymeric/latex coatings that form a strong chemical and physical bonds with the cementitious matrix, leading to a denser interfacial transition zone and enhanced formation of the hydration product (C–S–H gel) [ 28 , 54 , 62 , 63 , 119 ]. However, the same surface modifications that boost mechanical properties concurrently reduce fresh-state workability (slump and flowability): rougher fibers generate higher frictional resistance during mixing, coated fibers increase bulk density and alter hydrophilicity, and enhanced early fiber-matrix adhesion impedes particle movement [ 27 , 28 , 54 , 62 , 63 , 119 , 145 ]. While untreated fibers also reduce workability, treated fibers often exacerbate this effect, requiring superplasticizers or mix adjustments to maintain adequate flow [ 148 ]. Thus, a fundamental trade-off exists—superior interfacial bonding from fiber treatments inevitably compromises workability, a consistent finding across dosages and treatment methods [ 95 ,  96 – 97 , 99 , 100 , 133 ,  134 – 135 ].

The incorporation of sisal fibers into concrete generally affects workability, with both untreated and treated fibers often reducing flowability and slump. Alkali treatments, such as NaOH and Na₂CO₃, tend to slightly reduce slump and flowability due to increased surface roughness and fiber-matrix adhesion [ 24 , 35 , 88 ]. Similarly, polymeric and latex-based coatings, while enhancing mechanical performance, can also reduce workability by increasing bulk density and fiber-matrix interaction [ 88 , 86 , 87 ]. Untreated sisal fibers typically decrease workability as well, often requiring the use of superplasticizers or admixtures to maintain adequate flow, especially at higher fiber content [ 23 , 113 ]. Physical treatments such as boiling, washing, or wetting-drying cycles have been shown in some cases to improve workability by modifying fiber surfaces [ 114 ] while thermal treatments like autoclaving can slightly reduce workability, depending on changes in fiber morphology [ 45 , 54 ]. Overall, the incorporation of sisal fibers into concrete consistently reduces concrete workability with the extent depending on fiber type, treatment method, dosage, and the use of chemical admixtures to compensate for flow loss.

The inclusion of sisal fibers, whether untreated or treated, generally reduces concrete workability, with the extent of the reduction influenced by fiber content, treatment, and orientation. Untreated fibers consistently decrease slump and flowability, particularly at higher dosages, due to their hydrophilic nature and tendency to agglomerate, which affects cement consistency and increases water demand [ 62 , 115 ,  116 – 117 ]. Physical treatments, such as wetting-drying cycles on sisal residues, can modify fiber morphology and improve bonding; however, their effects on workability are not always quantified [ 118 ]. Chemical treatments, including urea, EDTA, ammonium, NaOH, and acetic acid, primarily enhance fiber-matrix interface and mechanical properties, with minimal or unreported impacts on workability [ 11 , 61 , 107 ]. High fiber contents or untreated fibers often require adjustments to water or the use of superplasticizers to maintain adequate flowability [ 117 ]. Additives such as styrene-acrylic copolymer and micro silica can help optimize workability while protecting fibers and improving durability [ 39 ]. Overall, the findings are summarized in Table  2 , which shows that fiber content and surface characteristics remain the dominant factors affecting concrete workability, while proper mix adjustments are essential when incorporating sisal fibers [ 94 ,  95 ,  96 ,  97 ,  98 ,  99 ,  100 – 101 ]. Based on synthesized data from 23 studies to provide the following mix adjustment guidance. The Mix Adjustment matrix the required superplasticizer (SP) dosage can be estimated using the empirical relationship: SP Dosage (%) = 0.5 + 0.015 × (FC × 100) × (1 + 0.3 × (TS/100–1)) where FC is fiber content (wt% of cement) and TS is targeting slump (mm). at 1.5% fiber content targeting 120 mm slump, this yields approximately 2.9% SP (PCE-based), with adjustment factors for treatment type: untreated/horrified (AF = 1.0), silane-treated (AF = 1.1), alkali-treated (AF = 1.15–1.25), and coated fibers (AF = 1.05–1.15). Alternatively, water-to-binder ratio can be increased by 0.02–0.03 for 1.0% fiber content, 0.04–0.06 for 1.5%, and 0.07–0.10 for 2.0% (though > 1.5% is not recommended for routine applications). Pre-wetting fibers for 15–30 min at 20–30% of fiber weight improves workability by 10–15%. For standard construction (slump 75–100 mm), recommended SP dosages are: 0.8–1.2% for 1.0% untreated fibers, 1.2–1.8% for 1.0% treated fibers, 1.2–1.8% for 1.5% untreated fibers, and 1.8–2.5% for 1.5% treated fibers. For self-compacting concrete (slump 100–150 mm), the corresponding dosages are 1.2–1.8%, 1.5-2.0%, 1.8–2.5%, and 2.5-3.0%, respectively. Quality control should include slump measurements at 0, 15, and 60 min to verify workability retention, with acceptance criteria of ≤ 10% slump loss at 15 min and ≤ 25% at 60 min.

sections.heading: Water absorption
paragraphs: Sisal fibers naturally exhibit high hydrophilicity due to abundant hydroxyl groups in their cellulose and hemicellulose components, which generally increases water absorption in concrete when the fibers are used untreated. Studies have shown that untreated sisal fibers lead to higher water uptake, especially at higher dosages or when fibers cluster in the mix, creating voids and capillary channels that facilitate water penetration [ 106 , 119 , 74 ]. This elevated water absorption can reduce concrete durability by increasing susceptibility to shrinkage cracking, freeze-thaw damage, and chemical attacks such as acid or sulfate ingress. To mitigate this issue, chemical treatments are widely employed, including alkali (NaOH), silane coupling agents, urea, EDTA, ammonium salts, and esterification. These treatments modify the fiber surface, reduce hydrophilicity, and improve fiber-matrix bonding, resulting in lower water absorption and enhanced long-term durability [ 9 , 107 ]. For example, alkali and silane treatments not only roughen the fiber surface for better adhesion but also form a partial hydrophobic barrier to water ingress [ 120 ]. Similarly, polymeric coatings (e.g., carboxylated styrene-butadiene rubber), natural rubber latex, and paraffin oil reduce fiber porosity and water absorption while simultaneously improving mechanical performance [ 36 , 86 , 84 ]. Physical treatments such as wetting-drying cycles or Hornification increase the dimensional stability of fibers and reduce their swelling capacity, thereby indirectly lowering water uptake [ 121 , 46 ]. Hybrid approaches that combine chemical treatment with fiber orientation control or additional surface coatings further improve resistance to water penetration by creating a denser and more uniform fiber-matrix interface, minimizing the micro-voids that otherwise act as water pathways [ 77 , 122 ]. In addition to fiber treatments, the use of admixtures such as superplasticizers or micro silica helps maintain workability while reducing water absorption by improving fiber dispersion and minimizing micro-void formation around individual fibers [ 117 , 39 ]. Micro silica, in particular, acts as a pore filler and pozzolan, refining the matrix structure and reducing permeability. Overall, controlling water absorption in sisal fiber-reinforced concrete requires a combination of fiber surface treatment, optimal fiber dosage, and complementary admixtures to enhance both mechanical properties and durability. As summarized in Table  2 , the effect of water absorption is directly related to the overall performance of sisal fiber-reinforced concrete, especially in terms of long-term durability a relationship further detailed in Table eight of the original review. Future research should focus on quantifying the relative efficiency of different treatment methods under long-term water exposure and developing standardized water absorption test protocols specifically for natural fiber-reinforced cementitious composites.

sections.heading: Compressive strength
paragraphs: Numerous studies have demonstrated that incorporating natural fibers can enhance the compressive strength of concrete and cementitious composites under optimal conditions. T. Amsalu Fode et al. [ 9 ] reported significant strength gains using treated fibers, while [ 113 , 127 ] also observed notable improvements attributed to fiber treatment and optimized content. Similarly, studies by [ 128 , 23 , 129 ] and [ 24 ] confirmed that compressive strength is enhanced when fiber volume is carefully controlled, as shown in Fig.  16 . Additional positive outcomes were reported by [ 35 , 37 , 89 , 125 ] and all emphasized the mechanical benefits of natural fibers. On the other hand [ 86 , 87 ] and [ 125 ], observed no significant change in compressive strength, indicating that fiber inclusion can be mechanically neutral under certain conditions.
Fig. 16 compressive strength of concrete with the addition of sisal fiber [ 88 ]

As noted by some authors, the addition of sisal fibers to concrete can sometimes reduce compressive strength. This is primarily attributed to poor fiber-matrix bonding and non-uniform fiber dispersion, which create weak zones within the composite. For instance [ 106 , 84 , 119 , 43 ], and [ 92 ] all documented compressive strength losses, highlighting the importance of fiber treatment and mix design. In contrast, several research works, such as [ 36 , 86 , 121 , 107 , 70 , 46 , 62 ] and [ 44 ] focused on other performance aspects, such as flexural strength, toughness, thermal properties, and fiber-matrix bonding, without clearly reporting compressive strength results, and the summary is presented in Table  3 .

Most studies do not support the use of untreated sisal fiber, as untreated fibers often contain surface impurities such as wax, lignin, and hemicellulose that hinder adhesion to the cement paste, increasing porosity in the interfacial transition zone. Furthermore, the most likely cause of strength reduction is fiber clustering or balling during mixing, which can disrupt concrete homogeneity, leading to stress concentrations and microcracks under load. Consequently, the overall compressive strength of sisal fiber-reinforced concrete may decrease compared with plain concrete [ 87 , 48 , 128 ] and [ 17 ].

Table  4  summarizes the findings from different studies and clearly shows that the effect of fiber addition is dosage-dependent, with the optimum range generally lying between 1% and 1.5% by volume. At very low dosages (< 1%), the improvements are inconsistent. For instance, a 0.2% dosage resulted in a noTable 14.9% increase, while 0.5–0.8% additions showed only 2–7% improvement, suggesting that performance at these levels is heavily influenced by fiber dispersion and matrix interactions. The most consistent and significant gains were observed at moderate dosages of 1–1.5%, where compressive strength improvements range from about 14% to 40.15%, indicating that this is the “sweet spot” for effective crack bridging and stress redistribution without compromising workability. At higher dosages beyond 2%, the data are limited, but the available results suggest diminishing returns due to fiber agglomeration and reduced compaction efficiency. Overall, the results show that sisal fibers can significantly enhance compressive strength by up to 40.15% when used at an optimal level, with excessive or insufficient additions leading to weaker or inconsistent performance (Fig.  17 ).

The regression analysis shows that adding sisal fiber addition can positively influence the compressive strength of SFRC, with R² values ranging from 0.9369 to 0.9540, confirming a strong correlation. Regression slopes of  +  2.34 and  +  0.1457 indicate that fiber addition enhances compressive strength, with improvements of up to 2.34% per unit increase in fiber content.

sections.heading: Flexural Strength
paragraphs: Several studies have demonstrated that sisal fibers act as effective crack-arresting agents, improving the flexural response of cement composites when used at optimal quantities, as shown in Figs.  8  and  14 . For example, Z. Zhang et al. [ 157 ] reported that untreated sisal fibers, incorporated at 0.5–2% by volume, significantly enhanced flexural performance, with an optimum content of about 1–1.5%. Beyond this range, excessive fiber addition led to agglomeration and poor fiber dispersion, negatively affecting workability and causing un even stress distribution between fibers and matrix, ultimately reducing flexural strength. Similarly, G.Z Guizzardi et al. [ 119 ] confirmed that while flexural strength increased at moderate dosages, higher fiber contents adversely affected consistency due to the high water uptake of untreated fibers.

In most studies, flexural strength is directly related to treatments applied to sisal fibers, and these studies show that treatments have distinct impacts on the flexural performance of concrete. SEM analysis in Fig.  18  shows that alkali-modified sisal fibers (M-SF-AM-1) produced weaker mortar due to internal stresses, micro cracks, and poor adhesion at the interface, which reduced the fibers’ ability to control crack propagation. In contrast, treatments such as urea (UR) and EDTA improved fiber matrix bonding and supported better hydration, allowing the fibers to bridge cracks more effectively. This enhanced crack-bridging capacity directly contributes to higher flexural strength, making the concrete more resistant to bending loads and improving its overall durability [ 70 ]. demonstrated that chemical treatments using urea, EDTA, and ammonium solutions created a denser fiber matrix interface, reducing porosity and enhancing load transfer, which led to notable gains in flexural resistance, as shown in Fig.  19 . Similarly [ 107 ], applied esterification with acyl chlorides, which not only reduced fiber moisture absorption but also altered fiber morphology, thereby enhancing stability and flexural load capacity over time. On the physical treatment side [ 74 ], showed that thermomechanical pulping of sisal fibers improved fracture toughness and flexural strength by refining fiber surfaces and increasing interfacial bonding.
Fig. 18 SEM images of mortar containing treated and untreated fibers [ 70 ]
Fig. 19 flexural strength of concrete using treated sisal fiber

Despite these improvements, untreated fibers are susceptible to degradation in the highly alkaline cementitious environment. Filho et al. [ 43 ] Investigated ageing and degradation and reported that untreated fibers gradually lost structural integrity, leading to reductions in flexural capacity with long-term exposure. This degradation is attributed to the dissolution of hemicellulose and lignin, which weakens fiber-matrix adhesion and reduces load transfer efficiency. Treatments that protect fibers from alkalinity therefore play a crucial role in maintaining flexural strength throughout the composite’s service life. Across the literature, sisal fibers demonstrate consistent improvements in flexural strength, typically ranging from 10 to 30% at optimal dosages. The positive effect is amplified by chemical or physical treatments that enhance fiber matrix bonding and limit durability concerns. These findings underline that sisal fiber not only contributes to crack bridging but also significantly improves the ductility and toughness of cementitious composites [ 10 , 135 , 36 , 136 , 137 , 138 ].

As shown in Table  5 , the summary of results from various authors on the flexural strength of sisal fiber reinforced concrete (SFRC) demonstrates that the inclusion of sisal fibers markedly enhances performance. However, the degree of improvement is highly influenced by fiber dosage and mix proportions. The optimum fiber dosage generally falls between 1% and 2% by volume, where the most notable improvements are observed. For example, an increase of 88.8% at 1.5% fiber content [ 81 ] 84.7% at 2% [ 134 ] and 68.5% at 1.5% [ 9 ]. Demonstrate the substantial role of fibers in bridging cracks and improving ductility. Moderate gains are also seen at lower dosages, such as 19.1% at 0.75% [ 139 ] and 18% at 1% [ 80 ], confirming that even small additions improve flexural resistance.

However, some studies reported minimal enhancement, such as only 1.8% improvement at 1% fiber dosage [ 135 ] and 3.08% at 1% [ 34 ], likely due to variations in fiber treatment, dispersion, or matrix compatibility. At higher dosages, performance does not always increase further, as shown by 21.75% at 4% fiber addition [ 23 ], indicating that excessive fiber content can cause clustering and reduce efficiency. Overall, the findings highlight that 1–2% sisal fiber is the most effective range for improving flexural strength, with possible enhancements of more than 80%.

Similarly, Fig.  20  summarizes the flexural results, and clearly shows that the addition of sisal fibers can substantially enhance the flexural strength of concrete when used at suitable dosages. The strongest trends appear in the models with positive slopes, such as Y = 3x + 33.217, Y = 3x + 33.217, Y = 3x + 33.217 (R 2  = 0.9854 R 2  = 0.9854 R 2  = 0.9854) and Y = 5.9015x + 4.8402, Y = 5.9015x + 4.8402, y = 5.9015x + 4.8402 (R 2  = 0.9419 R 2  = 0.9419 R 2  = 0.9419), which indicate consistent improvements in flexural performance as fiber content increases. These results highlight that moderate fiber additions, particularly around 1–2% by volume, provide reliable strength gains by improving crack resistance and load redistribution. The high R 2  values confirm that these improvements are well supported by experimental data, making sisal fiber an effective reinforcement for enhancing concrete’s flexural capacity.

sections.heading: Split tensile strength
paragraphs: As with flexural strength, the incorporation of sisal fibers has been widely reported to enhance the split tensile strength of concrete. One study observed that both sisal and bamboo fibers increased the split tensile resistance of concrete compared to control specimens [ 128 ], while another confirmed that sisal fiber incorporation simultaneously improved compressive, tensile, and flexural strength, with tensile strength showing the most pronounced gains [ 125 ]. Regarding treatment effects, an evaluation of NaOH and acetic acid treatments noted that although untreated fibers improved tensile strength due to their natural roughness and bonding ability, treated fibers exhibited better compatibility and reduced long-term deterioration [ 62 ]. Additionally, the addition of styrene-acrylic copolymer and micro silica alongside sisal fibers not only enhanced compressive and flexural strength but also significantly increased tensile strength while reducing water absorption [ 71 ]. Overall, tensile strength improvements range from 15% to 35%, depending on fiber dosage and treatment method. However, a major drawback of sisal fiber addition is its negative effect on workability, which indirectly influences tensile performance. One of the studies reported reduced workability with increasing fiber content due to the high surface area and water absorption capacity of fibers [ 18 ], while another further demonstrated that untreated sisal fibers substantially reduced flowability, increased yield stress, and raised plastic viscosity, leading to poor compaction and uneven fiber distribution within the matrix [ 117 ]. This workability challenge means that without the use of admixtures such as polycarboxylate-based superplasticizers the potential tensile strength improvements may not be fully realized. Durability also plays a critical role in retaining tensile strength over time. Subjecting fibers to wetting-drying cycles improved their dimensional stability and preserved tensile performance over time [ 121 ], and protective treatments using styrene-acrylic copolymer and micro silica prevented alkaline degradation, thereby sustaining tensile gains over longer durations [ 71 ]. This highlights the importance of treatments not only for enhancing short-term performance but also for ensuring long-term structural reliability of fiber-reinforced composites. In summary, split tensile strength consistently improves with sisal fiber incorporation, particularly at fiber volume fractions of 1–1.5%, with reported gains generally between 15% and 35%. However, some research reported gains of less than 15% and above 50%, as shown in Table  6 . Furthermore, Table  7  in the original review summarizes the findings of different authors regarding the reasons for improvement of sisal fiber-reinforced concrete with various additions of treated sisal fiber.

According to the studies, tensile strength improvement in sisal fiber reinforced concrete is mainly due to better fiber matrix bonding (through surface treatments that increase roughness and remove weak layers), effective crack-bridging that enhances ductility, the use of protective coatings and additives that improve durability, and maintaining an optimum fiber dosage to ensure good dispersion without clustering. These factors together lead to stronger interfacial stability and more efficient stress transfer [ 23 , 35 , 88 , 89 , 86 , 121 , 46 ] and [ 70 ].

[ 124 ][ 113 ] Optimized fiber dosage (low % fibers gave best tensile improvements, avoiding clustering) [ 107 ][ 128 ][ 71 ][ 119 ] Increased interfacial stability & durability (esterification, urea/EDTA, general chemical treatments)

Both flexural and split tensile strengths show significant and consistent improvements when sisal fibers are incorporated into cementitious composites, with flexural gains of 10–30% and split tensile gains of 15–35% reported across a wide range of studies, primarily due to the fibers’ ability to bridge propagating cracks, transfer tensile stress across crack faces, dissipate energy through pull-out and debonding, and promote multi-cracking behavior at optimal fiber contents [ 10 , 15 , 143 , 144 , 24 , 77 , 80 , 81 , 83 , 85 , 135 , 136 ]. The underlying mechanisms are well established: when a tensile or bending load is applied, microcracks initiate at stress concentrations; sisal fibers oriented perpendicular or inclined to the crack plane act as mechanical bridges, carrying load across the crack and reducing the stress intensity at the crack tip, thereby delaying crack propagation and allowing the composite to sustain load beyond the point where plain concrete would fail catastrophically. Additionally, as fibers deboned and slide against the cementitious matrix, they absorb substantial energy, contributing to the characteristic post-crack ductility and increased toughness of sisal-reinforced concrete. At optimal fiber dosages, well-dispersed fibers can even produce multiple fine cracks rather than a single dominant crack—a phenomenon known as pseudo-strain hardening which further enhances strain capacity and tensile strength. The effectiveness of fiber addition is, however, highly dosage-dependent, with an optimal range consistently identified between 0.8% and 1.5% by volume of concrete, where well-dispersed fibers effectively bridge cracks and improve stress transfer. Concrete evidence from the literature supports this window: for example, tensile strength increased by 52.3% at 1.5% fiber content 52.3% at 1.5% fiber content [ 81 ], 45% at 0.8% [ 35 ], and 38.9% at 1.5% [ 60 ]. These figures demonstrate that moderate fiber additions provide the greatest reinforcement efficiency, as the inter-fiber spacing becomes small enough to intersect most potential crack planes without causing excessive fiber contact or clustering. At very low dosages (below 0.5% by volume), the effect is minimal because the fiber volume fraction is insufficient to provide continuous crack bridging across the matrix; for instance, only a 5.21% improvement in tensile strength was recorded at 0.5% fiber content [ 41 ]. Conversely, at high dosages (2% or more by volume), performance declines significantly due to fiber clumping and balling during mixing, poor dispersion, increased porosity from entrapped air and inadequate compaction, and severely reduced workability, all of which introduce defects rather than reinforcement yielding only modest gains such as 9.01% at 2% [164] and 12.23% at 1.5% under certain fiber types or conditions [ 54 ]. Fiber treatment plays a critical role in achieving and sustaining these strength improvements. Untreated sisal fibers can initially enhance tensile and flexural strength due to their natural surface roughness, which provides mechanical interlocking with the cement matrix, and their relatively high intrinsic tensile strength of 200–400 MPa [ 84 ]. However, untreated fibers suffer from two major drawbacks that severely limit long-term performance: high water absorption capacity leading to swelling, shrinkage, and matrix microcracking, and alkaline degradation in the high-pH cement pore solution (pH 12–13), which progressively dissolves lignin and hemicellulose, causing fiber mineralization, embrittlement, and loss of tensile capacity [ 84 ]. Chemical treatments such as NaOH (alkali), silane coupling agents, esterification, urea, and EDTA modify the fiber surface by removing waxes, oils, and amorphous components, exposing a roughened cellulose surface that increases mechanical bonding and provides more sites for chemical adhesion (e.g., hydrogen bonding with calcium silicate hydrate) [ 6 ,  84 ,  141 ].

These treatments also reduce hydrophilicity, thereby lowering water absorption and mitigating swelling-shrinkage cycles, and create a partial protective barrier against alkaline attack, leading to better fiber-matrix compatibility and sustained tensile gains over time. Protective admixtures, particularly the combination of styrene-acrylic copolymer and micro silica, have been shown to further enhance tensile strength by multiple mechanisms: the styrene-acrylic copolymer forms a flexible, water-resistant film around fibers and within the matrix, improving adhesion, reducing water penetration, and providing a physical barrier against alkaline ions; micro silica (silica fume), as a highly reactive pozzolan, consumes calcium hydroxide the primary source of alkalinity and produces additional calcium silicate hydrate, thereby lowering the pH of the pore solution, refining the pore structure, and reducing permeability [ 91 ]. Together, these admixtures not only increase short-term tensile strength but also prevent long-term alkaline degradation, ensuring that tensile gains are sustained over extended periods. Despite these advantages, a major and consistent drawback of adding sisal fiber is the reduction in workability, which indirectly limits the achievable tensile strength.

The high surface area and water absorption capacity of sisal fibers increase the yield stress and plastic viscosity of fresh concrete, substantially reducing flowability and slump, and leading to poor compaction, entrapped air, and uneven fiber distribution if not properly compensated [ 22 , 148 ]. Poor compaction creates voids that act as stress concentrators, while uneven fiber distribution results in some regions with insufficient reinforcement and others with fiber clumps that behave as defects. Consequently, without the use of high-range water-reducing admixtures (superplasticizers), such as polycarboxylate-based products, the potential tensile improvements from sisal fibers may not be fully realized, because proper fiber dispersion and matrix densification are essential for effective stress transfer and crack bridging [ 22 , 148 ].

Durability also plays a critical role in maintaining tensile strength over time, especially in structural applications where long-term reliability is paramount. Physical treatments such as wetting-drying cycles—a process known as Hornification improve the dimensional stability of sisal fibers by reducing irreversible swelling and increasing cellulose crystallinity, thereby preserving tensile performance over time [ 151 ]. Additionally, protective treatments using a styrene-acrylic copolymer and micro silica have been shown to prevent alkaline degradation and sustain tensile gains over longer durations, as confirmed by durability testing [ 91 ].

These findings underscore that fiber treatments and admixtures are important not only for enhancing short-term mechanical properties but also for ensuring the long-term structural reliability of sisal fiber-reinforced composites. In summary, sisal fibers consistently and significantly enhance split tensile and flexural strength at optimal dosages of 0.8–1.5% by volume, with reported tensile gains of 15–35% and flexural gains of 10–30%. However, achieving these improvements requires a holistic approach that includes appropriate fiber treatment (chemical, physical, or hybrid), workability adjustment with superplasticizers to ensure uniform dispersion and proper compaction, and durability protection through pozzolans or polymer coatings to mitigate alkaline degradation and dimensional instability. Collectively, the evidence demonstrates that sisal fiber is a sustainable, cost-effective, and ecologically favorable reinforcement material that enhances ductility, toughness, and durability in concrete and mortar applications when properly implemented with appropriate treatments and mix design adjustments.

sections.heading: Durability of sisal fiber reinforced concrete
paragraphs: Despite these advances, the durability of sisal fiber-reinforced cement composites remains a critical challenge, particularly with regard to water absorption, chloride-ion permeability, resistance to acid attack, and thermal stability [ 148 , 149 , 57 , 150 ]. As shown in Fig.  22 , the alkaline environment of cement matrices induces fiber degradation through mineralization and hydrolysis, compromising long-term performance [ 57 , 43 ]. While chemical and physical treatments such as alkali, silane, and esterification have been proposed to mitigate these effects, their comparative effectiveness and environmental impacts are not fully understood [ 9 ,  107 ,  89 , 120 ]. Contrasting findings exist regarding untreated sisal fibers, with some studies reporting increased permeability and mass loss, whereas others highlight improvements in toughness and ductility when combined with biomimetic agents or hybrid fibers [ 23 , 148 ], and [ 151 ].

Fig. 22 SEM micrographs of the fracture surface of the aged concrete reinforced with Na2CO3-treated sisal fiber after 30 wet/dry cycles: ( a ) the sediment layer around sisal fiber, and ( b ) cross-section of sisal fiber [ 108 ]

This controversy underscores a significant knowledge gap in optimizing sisal fiber treatment and composite formulation to balance mechanical enhancement and durability [ 86 , 133 ]. Failure to close this gap continues to hinder the wider adoption of sisal fiber composites in structural applications. Nonetheless, some studies [ 45 , 53 , 108 , 152 ] have reported encouraging improvements in durability. For instance, as illustrated in Fig.  22 , a protective layer of calcium carbonate gradually deposits on the fiber surface, effectively sealing surface pits and pores (Figure.  22 a). This natural coating acts as a barrier against the highly alkaline environment produced during cement hydration. Remarkably, the alkalinity of concrete itself helps stabilize this layer, allowing it to remain intact over time and safeguard the internal fiber structure. Consequently, the breakdown of lignin and hemicellulose in the middle lamellae, as well as the alkaline-induced hydrolysis of cellulose molecules, is significantly minimized (Figure.  22 b). This protective mechanism plays a crucial role in enhancing the long-term integrity of sisal fibers embedded in concrete. Additionally, the calcium carbonate layer prevents harmful sodium ions from penetrating into concrete, minimizing the risk of alkali aggregate reactions. This illustrates that sisal fibers can provide long-term durability in concrete, protecting both the fibers and the surrounding matrix from chemical degradation.

The conceptual framework for this review integrates the properties of sisal fibers, such as hydrophilicity, tensile strength, and thermal resistance, with the cement matrix’s characteristics, including alkalinity and porosity [ 159 , 119 , 121 ]. The interaction at the fiber-matrix interface governs composite performance, and is influenced by fiber treatment methods that modify surface chemistry and dimensional stability [ 86 , 87 ]. Understanding these relationships is essential to developing durable, high-performance sisal fiber-reinforced cementitious composites [ 89 , 120 ].
