sections.heading: Fiber matrix interface quality
paragraphs: Among the selected articles, about twenty studies consistently reported that chemical treatments (alkaline, silane, polymer coatings), physical treatments (Hornification, autoclave), and hybridization improve fiber–matrix adhesion by increasing surface roughness, reducing hydrophilicity, and promoting chemical bonding [ 23 , 9 , 86 , 87 , 13 , 64 , 66 , 70 , 120 ]. Conversely, some studies showed that untreated sisal fibers exhibit poor bonding and durability due to swelling and alkaline degradation [ 148 , 133 , 86 , 87 ]. Improved interfacial quality correlates with enhanced mechanical properties, toughness, and durability.

As shown in Fig.  23 , fibrillation and calcium hydroxide deposition on the fiber surface increase the superficial roughness, thereby improving interlocking with the cement matrix. However, a low level of chemical treatment (e.g., 1 wt% alkali) does not provide sufficient roughness to enhance interfacial bonding, and higher water uptake can further reduce fiber–matrix adhesion. In contrast, fibers treated with an optimal dosage (e.g., 5 wt% alkali) exhibit the best interfacial performance, with improved fiber matrix bonding. This clearly shows how controlled chemical treatment can enhance the bond strength between sisal fibers and the cementitious matrix.
Fig. 23 Summary of the pullout test results of untreated and alkali-treated sisal fibers [ 157 ]

Measurement methods for chloride permeability, acid attack resistance, and thermal stability varied considerably across the literature, contributing to inconsistencies in reported durability outcomes. Chloride permeability was most commonly assessed using the rapid chloride penetration test (RCPT) in accordance with ASTM C1202, though some studies employed natural diffusion methods in NaCl solutions (0.1–1 M) over 3 to 12 months, reporting chloride diffusion coefficients ranging from 10⁻¹² to 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s [ 27 ,  120 , 150 ]. However, wide variations in NaCl concentration and frequent omissions of temperature control led to significant discrepancies. Acid attack resistance was typically evaluated by immersing specimens in sulfuric, hydrochloric, or acetic acid solutions at pH levels between 1 and 4 for periods of 7 to 90 days, with mass loss, strength reduction, or degradation depth recorded as metrics [ 27 , 7 ]; yet the type and concentration of acid, as well as the lack of continuous pH monitoring, led to poor comparability across studies. Thermal stability was primarily characterized using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential thermal analysis (DTA), or differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 5–20 °C/min up to 800 °C, often in nitrogen or air atmospheres, reporting onset degradation temperatures (typically 200–300 °C) and residue percentages [ 6 , 46 , 62 , 63 , 101 ]. The choice of heating rate and atmosphere significantly affected degradation peak positions and mass loss values, further complicating direct comparisons. Notably, several studies failed to report basic testing parameters such as temperature control, solution renewal frequency, or sample preconditioning, highlighting an urgent need for standardized durability assessment protocols for sisal fiber-reinforced cementitious composites (Table  13 ).

sections.heading: Microstructure of concrete
paragraphs: One of the most consistent findings across the literature is the role of matrix densification in improving fiber–matrix bonding [ 88 ]. observed the presence of portlandite, quartz, and C–S–H phases which formed a denser microstructure around treated fibers. As shown in Fig.  24 a and b) [ 108 ]. similarly, it showed that metakaolin and nano clay reduced calcium hydroxide and ettringite formation, thereby refining the interfacial zone through Pozzolanic reactions [ 89 ]. confirmed densification when alkali treatment and wastewater recycling were applied, with SEM, EDS, and XRD confirming structural improvements. Likewise [ 75 ], demonstrated that combining fibers with rice husk ash produced a denser matrix, reducing seepage and cracks. Collectively, these studies suggest that Pozzolanic substitution and supplementary cementitious materials enhance the microstructure by suppressing weak crystalline phases and encouraging the growth of stable C–S–H gels.

As shown in Fig.  25 , treated sisal fiber-reinforced concrete at high magnification (×2,000) reveals that samples with higher fiber content (P3: 1.25% and P4: 1.5%) exhibit denser microstructures than those with lower fiber content samples (P1: 0.5% and P2: 1.0%) and the control (C). Increased density corresponds to reduced pore structures and more extensive formation of calcium silicate hydrate (C─S─H) crystals and calcium hydroxide (C─H) gel. These hydration products fill micro cracks and voids in concrete, enhancing durability and reducing permeability. Notably, at 1.5% fiber content, the pore network is effectively filled and bridged by the hydration products, thereby demonstrating improved microstructural integrity. Protective coatings on fibers also produce clear microstructural changes [ 88 ]. S. Castoldi [ 86 ] showed, using SEM and AFM, that polymeric coatings formed a distinct interfacial layer that improved adhesion while reducing water absorption [ 53 ]. confirmed by FTIR that resin coatings bonded firmly to the fiber surface, enhancing durability and reducing hydroxyl-ion penetration. S. Thepruttana et al. [ 36 ] reported that dual coatings reduced porosity at the interface, while [ 39 ] demonstrated that styrene-acrylic and micro silica layers improved adhesion in geopolymer concrete. These findings highlight that engineered coatings act as protective shells, physically and chemically stabilizing the fiber matrix interface against alkaline attack. Figure  26  shows gaps and voids between the uncoated sisal fiber and the cement matrix. Optical microscopy indicates that uncoated fibers exhibit poor adhesion, leading to internal pores that increase water absorption. In contrast, coated fibers form a strong bond with the cement matrix, reducing pore formation and water uptake. This enhanced interfacial bonding also improves the composite’s flexural strength. As observed in Fig.  26 , microscopic analysis highlights the critical role of fiber coating in promoting effective fiber matrix interaction, which directly influences the mechanical performance and durability of fiber reinforced cement composites [ 36 ].

Alkali treatments, however, yield mixed results. B.Bahja et al. [ 84 ] reported reductions in Ca (OH) ₂ and CaCO₃ peaks after NaOH and paraffin oil treatments, indicating modifications to fibre surface chemistry [ 24 ] and [ 106 ]. similarly observed significant morphological changes after alkali treatment. Yet older studies by [ 118 ] revealed porous, calcium hydroxide-rich transition zones that weakened bonding and reduced mechanical performance [ 153 , 13 , 64 ]. improved dimensional stability and bonding by altering fiber wall structures. These findings suggest that while alkali attack remains a major degradation pathway, it can be mitigated either by reducing portlandite or by stabilizing the fiber microstructure. Nanostructured modifications and mineral precipitation also enhance the microstructure [ 151 ]. confirmed nano-silica deposition on fibers, creating roughened surfaces and introducing chemically active bonding groups [ 35 ]. Further showed that Na₂CO₃ treatment enhanced durability by depositing calcium carbonate along the interface. These studies illustrate how nanotechnology and mineralization processes can actively functionalize the microstructure, improving both bonding and self-repair capacity. Another important microstructural aspect involves crack bridging and fiber matrix interaction [ 43 , 65 ]. quantified how irregular fiber cross-sections altered interfacial bonding and influenced tensile behaviour [ 37 ]. visualized fiber pull-out mechanisms and micro crack development, while [ 53 ] demonstrated that hybrid and sisal fibers altered crack propagation, enabling strain-hardening behaviour. These observations emphasize that the geometry and physical distribution of fibers strongly influence the microstructural mechanisms of fracture resistance.

The treatment of the fiber modifies its microstructure, as shown in Fig.  27 , resulting in a significant reduction in variation in the fiber’s cross-sectional area. This is because the drying process significantly reduces the large pores and the surface area. Finally, long-term durability studies reveal that microstructural changes persist with ageing [ 113 ]. showed that fibers degraded under alkaline conditions, with SEM capturing surface deterioration. By contrast [ 42 ], demonstrated that wet–dry cycles improved fiber matrix bonding and densified the microstructure [ 74 ]. found that partial debonding occurred at the interface, without excessive accumulation of portlandite, thereby improving compatibility. These results indicate that microstructural stability over time depends on controlling calcium hydroxide content, minimizing porosity, and preserving fiber morphology under environmental stressors.

Taken together, the evidence shows that the microstructural composition of fiber matrix composites is the primary determinant of their performance and durability. Treatments that densify the matrix, enhance C–S–H gel formation, or introduce protective coatings consistently improve interfacial stability. In contrast, untreated systems often exhibit porous, calcium hydroxide-rich transition zones that weaken bonding and accelerate degradation. Advanced approaches, such as nano silica deposition, calcium carbonate self-healing, and hybrid fiber integration point toward the development of multifunctional composites in which the microstructure is deliberately engineered for both strength and resilience. Ultimately, controlling microstructural evolution by minimizing portlandite, tailoring fiber surfaces, and optimizing fiber matrix interactions remains the most effective strategy for achieving durable, high-performance, and sustainable fiber-reinforced cementitious composites [ 26 , 77 , 78 , 80 , 82 , 143 , 144 , 158 ].

Matrix densification via pozzolanic reactions (e.g., silica fume, metakaolin, nano-silica) reduces calcium hydroxide (CH) content and refines the interfacial transition zone (ITZ) by promoting secondary C–S–H gel formation. This directly translates into measurable mechanical gains: silica fume at 20–25% increases bond strength by 170% and pullout energy by 250%; nano-silica coating on sisal fibers raises flexural strength by 9.8% and toughness by 40.5%; metakaolin combined with Recron fiber yields 6.9% higher compressive strength, 4.5% higher split-tensile strength, and 3.8% higher flexural strength. Protective polymer or nano-silica coatings act as alkaline barriers and adhesion promoters, reducing water absorption while increasing interfacial bond strength by up to 28% in pullout tests, with corresponding improvements in durability under wet–dry cycles (80–95% mechanical property regain) [ 10 , 24 , 159 ].

Alkali treatment of natural fibers removes surface impurities and improves wettability, boosting compressive strength by 30.6% (sisal) and split tensile strength by up to 2700% (abaca), though untreated systems with porous CH-rich ITZs weaken bonding. Hornification (wetting–drying cycles) closes large fiber pores, stabilizes cross-sectional area, and increases fiber–cement bond strength by 23%. Engineered fiber geometry matters: radial ITZ stiffness is 31% higher and ductility 28% greater than tangential directions, directly influencing crack bridging and pullout behavior. Hybrid fiber systems activate multi-scale crack control, raising compressive strength by 17.1% and achieving flexural toughness comparable to steel-only composites at lower dosages. Collectively, these quantitative links confirm that deliberate microstructural regulation minimizing portlandite, maximizing C–S–H, applying functional coatings, and optimizing hybridization is the primary driver of macroscopic performance and long-term durability in fiber-reinforced cementitious composites [ 24 , 80 , 85 , 160 ].

sections.heading: Energy and Viability of Common Surface Treatments on Sisal Fiber
paragraphs: Although the reviewed treatments (alkali [ 28 ,  140 ,  101 ,  62 ,  63 ,  118 ,  7 ,  139 ,  140 ], silane [ 120 ,  118 ], polymeric coatings [ 62 ,  63 ,  27 ,  46 ], Na₂CO₃ [ 54 ], esterification [ 141 ], pozzolanic/alkaline blends [ 142 ,  143 ,  7 ], and modifiers such as urea, EDTA, styrene-acrylic, and micro silica [ 90 ,  91 ]) demonstrably improve fiber–matrix adhesion, mechanical strength, and durability, their sustainability implications remain unquantified. For instance, alkali treatment with NaOH requires energy for solution preparation, heating (often 50–80 °C for 2–24 h), and multiple water rinses, generating alkaline wastewater that requires neutralization. Silane coupling agents involve organosilicon precursors synthesized energy-intensively from metallurgical-grade silicon (≈ 200 MJ/kg), and their hydrolysis step typically requires an ethanol–water mixture and elevated temperatures. Polymeric coatings (synthetic resins) contain petroleum-based compounds, the production of which emits 2–5 kg CO₂ per kg of resin. Even “greener” approaches such as Na₂CO₃ treatment or pozzolanic substitution (MgO–SiO₂, metakaolin) involve calcination or grinding steps with substantial embodied energy. Without a life cycle assessment (LCA) that reports MJ/kg of treated fiber and kg CO₂ per unit of performance improvement (e.g., per MPa of flexural strength gain), the field cannot ascertain whether these treatments yield net environmental benefits or merely shift burdens upstream.

From a biodegradability perspective, the very treatments that enhance composite durability often undermine the end-of-life advantage of sisal fibers. Untreated sisal degrades readily in moist soil or compost (50–70% mass loss in 60 days). However, alkali treatment, while removing hemicellulose and lignin, can create porous, calcium-rich transition zones [ 7 ] that entrap matrix hydrates, physically hindering microbial access to the fiber core. Silane and polymeric coatings [ 62 ,  63 ,  27 ,  46 ] intentionally form hydrophobic, crosslinked shells on fibers; these shells are not biodegradable and may persist as microplastics even if the sisal core eventually degrades. Esterification [ 141 ] chemically blocks hydroxyl groups, reducing moisture absorption—but moisture is essential for enzymatic hydrolysis, so modified fibers degrade much more slowly, if at all, in landfill conditions. Pozzolanic blends [ 142 ,  143 ,  7 ] lower matrix alkalinity to preserve fiber morphology, yet the densified interface reduces permeability, slowing water ingress and biological attack. None of the cited studies reports composite-scale biodegradation tests (e.g., ISO 20200 or ASTM D5338) or measures the ecotoxicity of degradation byproducts.

sections.heading: Limitations of the reviewed studies
paragraphs: Many studies on sisal fiber reinforced concrete are constrained by geographic and methodological limitations that reduce the generalizability of their findings. Research is often concentrated in specific regions, limiting understanding of how climatic and socioeconomic variations may influence fiber properties and performance. Additionally, small sample sizes, limited variations in fiber treatment, and short curing periods reduce the robustness and reproducibility of experimental results. Variability in fiber treatment methods, such as chemical, alkaline, pozzolanic, or thermal processes, further complicates comparisons of outcomes and makes it challenging to establish standardized best practices for enhancing durability and mechanical strength. Other limitations include a predominant focus on mechanical properties while neglecting broader factors such as environmental impact, economic feasibility, and social acceptance. Many studies also lack comprehensive long-term durability assessments under diverse ecological conditions, leaving questions about the real-world lifespan and performance of sisal fiber composites. Furthermore, variability in mix designs, fiber lengths, and volume fractions across studies hinders direct comparison and identification of optimal formulations. The scarcity of systematic cross-continental analyses limits the development of globally applicable guidelines for the effective use of sisal fiber in cementitious composites.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The following conclusions were drawn from the articles considered for this review:

Sisal fiber incorporation improves tensile, flexural, and impact resistance. Compressive strength gains range from 6% to up 40.15%, depending on fiber content, treatment, and orientation. Optimal performance is generally observed at 0.5% − 1.5% fiber dosage by weight of cement. Fiber length and orientation significantly influence composite performance. Chemical treatments improve fiber-matrix bonding, reduce water absorption, and increase durability. Physical modifications also enhance the mechanical and durability properties of the composites. Current studies often focus on short-term durability, with limited long-term performance data. Variability in fiber treatments and testing protocols leads to inconsistent results. Socio-economic and market-related analyses remain underexplored. Further research is needed to improve durability, standardize testing, and support large-scale global adoption.

sections.heading: Recommendation
paragraphs: Future research should prioritize the development of standardized, eco-friendly fiber treatment protocols to improve reproducibility and reduce environmental impacts. Long-term durability studies under diverse climatic conditions are necessary to validate real-world performance. Optimization of fiber content, length, and orientation should be undertaken to balance mechanical strength with workability across different concrete and mortar types. Comprehensive life cycle and environmental impact assessments are needed to quantify sustainability benefits, while socio-economic studies should evaluate market feasibility, policy frameworks, and adoption potential in both urban and rural contexts. Further exploration of hybrid fiber composites combining sisal with other natural or synthetic fibers could enhance mechanical and durability performance. Strengthening regional supply chains and processing infrastructure will support scalable implementation, while standardized mechanical testing and reporting methods are critical for comparability and global adoption. These measures collectively will facilitate wider, sustainable use of sisal fiber in cementitious construction materials. Given the geographic concentration of sisal fiber research in only a few countries (India, Brazil, and the United Kingdom) and the substantial regional variations in sisal species, harvesting methods, and processing conditions, the current body of evidence lacks generalizability. It is therefore recommended that future studies explicitly report geographic origin, agronomic practices, and processing parameters to enable cross-regional comparisons. More importantly, coordinated cross-regional comparative studies using standardized testing protocols should be prioritized. Establishing an open-access database that includes fiber properties alongside detailed metadata on species, harvest method, and processing conditions would further strengthen the field. Funding agencies and research networks are encouraged to support South-South collaborations among major sisal-producing countries (e.g., India, Brazil, Tanzania, China, Mexico) to address these gaps and improve the external validity of sisal fiber research.

Pozzolanic substitution with metakaolin/nano clay reduces Ca (OH)₂ and ettringite, densifying the matrix [ 10 ] Highlight that Pozzolanic treatments improve mechanical strength, while strong alkali causes environmental and degradation drawbacks.

Urea/EDTA treatments densify the interface, increasing hydrate development [ 70 ]. Styrene-acrylic and micro silica coatings enhance adhesion in geopolymer composites, reduce water absorption, and improve durability [ 71 ].
